accroche: One book tore down the reputation of an icon of anthropology. Since then, that book has collapsed too.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1928, the American anthropologist Margaret Mead published *Coming of Age in Samoa*, drawn from nine months of fieldwork carried out at age twenty-three. Her thesis: the torments of Western adolescence (crises, rebellion, sexual anxiety) are not a biological fatality of age. She sees them as the product of a particular upbringing. In Samoa, she writes, the transition is lived without the same drama, because society frames adolescent sexuality and the pressure on the individual differently. The book became a worldwide bestseller and one of the major arguments of the culturalist camp in the nature/nurture debate.

## A Book That Attacks Another

In 1983, five years after Mead's death, the New Zealand anthropologist Derek Freeman published *Margaret Mead and Samoa: The Making and Unmaking of an Anthropological Myth*. His charge is head-on: Mead lacked experience, never settled among the Samoans, and her biases skewed her conclusions; Samoan society is in reality competitive, violent, jealous, and adolescence there, far from peaceful, is trying. The *New York Times* gave the affair its front page on January 31, 1983. In public opinion, the news eclipses decades of Mead's work.

## The Hoax Comes Later

The story of the two young Samoan women, the one everyone remembers, is not in the 1983 book. It comes from an interview Freeman conducted in 1987 with Fa'apua'a Fa'amū, whom Mead had known in Samoa in 1926. Freeman drew from it a note published in 1989, then a second book in 1999, *The Fateful Hoaxing of Margaret Mead*: Mead was supposedly duped by two teenage girls who, as a joke, told her made-up stories about their sex lives.

The problem, documented by later re-readings of the record, is that this version does not hold up any better. Nothing establishes that Mead was “duped.” The accusation rests on a single passage, drawn from interviews that Freeman never published in full, and on a selective reading of Mead's work, more focused on her personal disqualification than on a rigorous re-examination of the Samoan data.

## What This Shifts

The episode does not invite us to pick a side, or to decide which of the two monographs finally tells the truth about Samoa. It invites us to be wary of one specific reflex: believing that a heavily publicized controversy necessarily settles a scientific debate. The story that circulated best, “Mead was exposed,” took hold far faster than its critical examination, which long remained confined to specialized journals.

What the story shifts, by implication, is also the question Mead herself asked: the share of the biological and the cultural in the adolescent experience cannot be settled by a single field study, however careful. Still less by refuting one study with another, fifty-five years later, with no new fieldwork to back it.

repere.texte: Margaret Mead and Samoa, published in 1983, five years after Mead's death, made the front page of the New York Times on January 31. The hoax accusation came only in 1989 and then 1999: sixteen years after the book it is attributed to, and both have been contested since.
repere.source: Derek Freeman, 1983 and 1999; Paul Shankman, Current Anthropology, 2013

carte.punch: Mead was “exposed.” The exposure did not hold up either.
carte.idee: Derek Freeman made the front page of the New York Times in 1983 by demolishing Margaret Mead's Samoan fieldwork, then accused her, sixteen years later, of having been duped by two teenage girls. Later re-readings showed that his charge, too, rested on fragile foundations.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Paul Shankman, “Mead–Freeman Controversy on Samoa,” The International Encyclopedia of Anthropology
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Standard academic overview of the controversy. Entry freely accessible, full text paywalled.

quiz.question: What do later re-readings of the Mead–Freeman controversy show?
choix: That Mead was entirely right and Freeman entirely wrong
That Freeman was right and Mead's work is worthless
That Freeman's charge also rested on fragile foundations
That the two studies dealt with two different islands
quiz.explication: Later work has shown that Freeman's accusation against Mead rested on fragile sources and a selective reading, without thereby validating the 1928 conclusions wholesale: the controversy does not close with a clear winner.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When was the hoax accusation against Margaret Mead made?
choix: In Freeman's book published in 1983, five years after Mead's death
In the front page of the New York Times of January 31, 1983
In a note in 1989, then in a second book in 1999
During Mead's lifetime, and she answered it before her death in 1978
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1983 book faults Mead for her inexperience and her biases. It does not accuse her of having been duped. The story of the two young Samoan women comes from an interview conducted in 1987, published in a note in 1989, then developed in a second book in 1999.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was the thesis of Coming of Age in Samoa, published by Mead in 1928?
choix: That the torments of adolescence stem from upbringing, not from age
That Samoan adolescence is more trying than in the West
That puberty occurs later in societies without writing
That Samoan society is competitive, violent, and jealous
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Mead argued that the crises of Western adolescence are not a biological fatality of age. She saw them as the product of a particular upbringing. The competitive society and trying adolescence are what Freeman described against her, fifty-five years later.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the hoax accusation rest on, according to the entry?
choix: On a new field study conducted in Samoa by Freeman in the 1980s
On a single passage from interviews never published in full
On Mead's field notebooks found after her death
On a public statement by the two Samoan women before the press
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Freeman never published the full text of his 1987 interviews with Fa'apua'a Fa'amū: the accusation rests on a single passage drawn from this material, and on a selective reading of Mead's work, focused on her personal disqualification.
